B.explanation: This is $60/80$ and compares the two balance lengths directly without subtracting to find the p.d. across $R_2$ alone.

C.explanation: This inverts the resistance ratio and treats $R_2$ as larger than $R_1$ although its balance difference of $20 \text{ cm}$ is smaller than $60 \text{ cm}$.

D.explanation: This is $80/60$ and compares total p.d. across $R_1+R_2$ with p.d. across $R_1$, not p.d. across $R_2$ with p.d. across $R_1$.

hints: Notice the left-hand end of the potentiometer wire is joined to the left-hand end of $R_1$, so a balance length measures potential drop from that common point.
Zero galvanometer current means $V_X$ equals the wire potential $60 \text{ cm}$ from the left, and $V_Y$ equals the wire potential $80 \text{ cm}$ from the left.
Because the wire is uniform, p.d. is proportional to length, so compare $I R_1$ with the $60 \text{ cm}$ length and $I(R_1+R_2)$ with the $80 \text{ cm}$ length to isolate $R_2$.
walkthrough: The lower cell sends the same current $I$ through $R_1$ and $R_2$ in series. Let the common left point be potential $V_0$.
At null, no current in the galvanometer so potentials are equal. Hence $V_0 - V_X$ equals the p.d. over $60 \text{ cm}$ of uniform wire, and $V_0 - V_Y$ equals the p.d. over $80 \text{ cm}$.
For uniform wire, p.d. $\propto$ length. Let wire p.d. per cm be $k$. Then $I R_1 = k \times 60$ and $I(R_1+R_2) = k \times 80$.
Thus $R_1 = 3R_2$, so the p.d. across $R_2$ corresponds to $80-60 = 20 \text{ cm}$ compared with $60 \text{ cm}$ for $R_1$.
